name: Fungible Token
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Any One Will Do: The Case for Interchangeable Value
lesson.summary: A fungible token is one where every unit is identical in value and function to every other unit of the same type, the same property that makes ordinary currency usable in the first place.
lesson.body:
Fungibility is a concept borrowed directly from traditional economics, and it describes something people already intuitively understand about money. Any genuine, valid one-dollar bill is worth exactly the same as any other one-dollar bill. Nobody cares which specific bill they receive in change, because the bills are functionally interchangeable. That interchangeability, applied to a digital token, is what fungibility means in a blockchain context: every unit of a fungible token is identical to every other unit, with no individual unit distinguishable from another in terms of value or function.

Most tokens built on blockchains are fungible, and the technical implementation reflects that directly. A fungible token contract, following a common interface such as Ethereum's widely used ERC-20 standard, does not track individual, uniquely identified units at all. It simply tracks a single number per address, the balance, and moves quantities between balances when transfers occur. There is no concept of token number 4,521 versus token number 4,522 within that balance, because such a distinction would be meaningless: any ten units are exactly as good as any other ten units.

This design choice is not incidental, it is what makes fungible tokens usable the way currencies and generic assets need to be usable. A stablecoin like one pegged to a national currency has to be fungible to function as a medium of exchange, because a merchant accepting payment needs to know that any unit received is worth exactly its face value, with no risk that a particular unit carries some different history or status than another. Fungibility is also what allows tokens to be pooled together in shared pools of liquidity on decentralized exchanges, where thousands of individual holders' contributions mix freely because no individual unit needs to be tracked or distinguished from the rest.

A concrete example helps ground this: suppose a wallet holds ten units of a fungible token used within some application, and sends five of them to a merchant in exchange for a service. The merchant does not receive five specific, individually identified tokens carrying some unique provenance; they simply receive an increase of five in their own balance as recorded by the contract, and could have received value from any other holder's balance with an identical outcome. This is precisely what makes fungible tokens well suited to acting as currency, reward points, or any other application where quantity, not individual identity, is what matters.

The value of understanding fungibility clearly becomes obvious as soon as it is contrasted with its opposite. Not every digital asset benefits from interchangeability. Some use cases specifically require that each unit be distinct and individually identifiable, which is exactly the gap that a different category of token, built to represent uniqueness rather than interchangeability, was designed to fill.
